question: Which brain regions are most consistently associated with major depressive disorder?
rawAnswer:
Across the curated records, the most consistently implicated region in major depressive disorder is the hippocampus, with bilateral volume reductions reported at a Moderate evidence level by three structural MRI sources: the ENIGMA MDD mega-analysis [study_schmaal_2016], an earlier meta-analysis reporting roughly 8% left and 10% right reductions that scaled with number of episodes [study_videbech_2004], and a cross-disorder meta-analysis in which hippocampal reduction was shared between PTSD and MDD [study_bromis_2018]. The anterior cingulate cortex is the next most convergent, also at Moderate level: rostral and caudal ACC show thinner cortex in adults with MDD [study_schmaal_2017], while resting-state work reports subregion-specific connectivity alterations — subgenual ACC with emotion-related regions, pregenual with sensorimotor, dorsal with cognition-related regions — a pattern coded as mixed in direction rather than uniformly reduced [study_zhou_2024], alongside reduced sgACC–amygdala connectivity in adults with recurrent MDD [study_fan_2025]. Note that the latter study found adolescent patients comparable to controls and cautioned that small samples inflate effects [study_fan_2025].

At the Emerging level, single records implicate the orbitofrontal cortex (lateral and medial), posterior cingulate and insula via reduced cortical thickness with small effect sizes (d -0.10 to -0.14) [study_schmaal_2017], the amygdala via reduced connectivity [study_fan_2025], and left middle frontal/DLPFC territory indirectly, where repetitive TMS was associated with a medium reduction in depressive symptoms (Hedges g -0.73) [study_kan_2023]. The EEG literature here disagrees and maps to no atlas region: one meta-analysis reported a small but significant frontal alpha asymmetry effect with high heterogeneity [study_luo_2025], whereas another found a negligible, non-significant effect with limited diagnostic value [study_vandervinne_2017]. Major depressive disorder is represented by 9 studies in this atlas (fMRI 2, sMRI 4, EEG 2, TMS 1) [corpus] — these counts describe the curated corpus, not the full literature, so absence of a region here should not be read as evidence against it.
